title: Chapter 3 Drill: Preconception Care, Prenatal Care, and Fetal Assessment

items.stem: A 28-year-old G1P0 woman has a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy at 20 weeks. One twin has a deepest vertical pocket of 1 cm with a small bladder, and the other has a pocket of 9 cm with a distended bladder. What is the best treatment?
options: Serial amnioreduction until term
Selective feticide of the larger twin
Fetoscopic laser ablation of the placental anastomoses
Maternal bed rest with hydration
items.explanation: This picture is twin-twin transfusion syndrome, stage II at least, and for stages II to IV before 26 weeks laser ablation of the communicating vessels improves survival compared with serial amnioreduction. Amnioreduction is a temporizing option when laser is unavailable. Selective reduction is reserved for specific complications. Bed rest and hydration do not alter the vascular connections that cause the imbalance.

items.stem: A 35-year-old G2P1 woman at 33 weeks receives indomethacin for tocolysis after a course of therapy for preterm labor. Which fetal finding is most likely if the drug is continued beyond 48 hours?
options: Oligohydramnios
Polyhydramnios
Macrosomia
Fetal tachycardia
items.explanation: Indomethacin lowers fetal urine output by reducing renal prostaglandins and can cause oligohydramnios, and it may constrict the ductus arteriosus, especially beyond 32 weeks. Polyhydramnios would suggest the opposite effect on fluid. Macrosomia is unrelated to this drug. Tachycardia is a known side effect of beta-agonist tocolytics rather than prostaglandin inhibitors. The other options address a different problem or risk harm.

items.stem: A 33-year-old G2P1 woman with blood type A negative and a negative antibody screen has vaginal bleeding at 9 weeks. A threatened abortion is diagnosed and the bleeding resolves. Her partner is Rh positive. What is the best next step regarding Rh status?
options: No immune globulin until the routine third trimester dose
Offer anti-D immune globulin
Check a Kleihauer-Betke test before deciding on any dose
Give anti-D only if she progresses to dilation and curettage
items.explanation: Bleeding with a threatened abortion is an event that can expose an Rh-negative woman to fetal cells, and anti-D immune globulin is reasonable and recommended by many authorities. Waiting until the routine 28-week dose leaves the exposure unprotected. Quantification testing is for large exposures late in pregnancy, not at 9 weeks. Intervention is not required for the indication.

items.stem: A 28-year-old G3P2 woman at 30 weeks asks about vaccinations. She had Tdap in her last pregnancy four years ago. What is the recommendation for this pregnancy?
options: No Tdap, because she is protected from the prior dose
Tdap only if the newborn will attend daycare
Tdap immediately after delivery instead of during pregnancy in the meantime
A Tdap dose between 27 and 36 weeks, ideally early in that window
items.explanation: Tdap is recommended with every pregnancy between 27 and 36 weeks to boost maternal antibody that crosses the placenta and protects the newborn against pertussis. Prior vaccination does not remove the need, because maternal antibody wanes within a year or two. Daycare attendance is irrelevant to the indication. Postpartum dosing leaves the infant unprotected in the first weeks, when pertussis is most dangerous.

items.stem: A 31-year-old G3P2 woman at 21 weeks has an ultrasound showing mild bilateral renal pelvis dilation of 5 mm and otherwise normal anatomy. What is the best management?
options: Immediate postnatal surgery planning without further evaluation
A follow-up ultrasound in the third trimester
Amniocentesis for karyotype only
Termination counseling
items.explanation: Mild renal pelvic dilation, once called pyelectasis, is a common soft finding that usually resolves, and a repeat scan in the third trimester is sufficient. Surgery is not planned because most cases are physiologic. Amniocentesis is not required for an isolated finding. Termination counseling is inappropriate, since the finding carries a very low risk and the great majority of fetuses are normal.

items.stem: A 26-year-old G1P0 woman at 20 weeks is found to be hepatitis B surface antigen positive on routine screening. She asks how to protect her baby. What is the best plan?
options: Give the infant vaccine alone at the 2 month visit
Recommend cesarean delivery to prevent transmission
Give hepatitis B immune globulin and the first vaccine dose to the infant within 12 hours of birth
Advise against breastfeeding
items.explanation: Perinatal transmission is prevented in most cases by hepatitis B immune globulin and the first vaccine dose within 12 hours after birth, followed by completion of the vaccine series. Delayed vaccination fails to protect the infant when the exposure occurs at delivery. Cesarean delivery does not lower transmission. Breastfeeding is permitted after the infant receives immunoprophylaxis.

items.stem: A 33-year-old G1P0 woman at 18 weeks has a thickened nuchal fold of 7 mm on anatomy ultrasonography. Her first-trimester screening was not done. What is the best next step?
options: Offer genetic counseling and diagnostic testing
Reassure her, since it is a normal variant without further evaluation
Repeat the scan in six weeks only
Schedule induction at 37 weeks
items.explanation: A thickened nuchal fold is the strongest second-trimester soft marker for Down syndrome and warrants counseling, with cell-free DNA screening or amniocentesis offered. Treating it as a normal variant ignores a significant risk. Repeating a scan alone does not provide a diagnosis. Early delivery is not part of management for a soft marker. The other options address a different problem or risk harm.

items.stem: A 36-year-old G2P1 woman at 17 weeks has a quadruple screen with low maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein, low unconjugated estriol, high human chorionic gonadotropin, and high inhibin A. Dating is confirmed by ultrasonography. Which aneuploidy does this pattern suggest?
options: Trisomy 18 with low levels of every analyte
Trisomy 21
Turner syndrome with cystic hygroma
Open neural tube defect with high alpha-fetoprotein
items.explanation: The classic Down syndrome pattern is low alpha-fetoprotein and estriol with elevated human chorionic gonadotropin and inhibin A. Trisomy 18 produces low levels of all analytes, including human chorionic gonadotropin. Turner syndrome with a hydrops picture can show high gonadotropin but is not the classic pattern. An open neural tube defect raises alpha-fetoprotein rather than lowering it.

items.stem: A 29-year-old G2P1 woman with a prior pregnancy affected by spina bifida presents for preconception counseling. She takes no medications and has a normal BMI. What daily folic acid dose should she begin at least one month before conception?
options: 0.4 mg
1 mg
4 mg
400 mg
items.explanation: A prior neural tube defect is the classic indication for high-dose supplementation, 4 mg daily starting at least one month before conception and continuing through the first trimester. The standard 0.4 mg dose is for average-risk women. One milligram does not meet the recommendation for recurrence risk reduction. A dose of 400 mg is a thousandfold error and is not used.

items.stem: A 29-year-old G2P1 woman who is Rh negative delivers an Rh-positive infant. A Kleihauer-Betke test estimates a fetomaternal hemorrhage of 60 mL of fetal whole blood. One vial of anti-D immune globulin covers 30 mL of fetal whole blood. How many vials should be given?
options: One vial
Two vials before any further testing
Six vials
Three vials
items.explanation: The standard calculation divides the estimated fetal whole blood volume by 30 mL, then adds one vial as a margin of error. Sixty divided by 30 is 2, plus one gives 3. One or two vials leave part of the exposure uncovered and risk alloimmunization. Six vials would result from multiplying instead of dividing, a calculation error that wastes product.

items.stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 woman at 34 weeks is evaluated for decreased fetal movement. A biophysical profile is performed. Which component is typically the last to be lost as fetal hypoxemia worsens?
options: Gross body movement
Reactive heart rate
Fetal breathing movements
Amniotic fluid volume
items.explanation: Fetal responses follow a hierarchy: the center regulating heart rate reactivity is affected first, followed by breathing, then movement, and finally tone, which is the last to disappear. Fluid volume reflects chronic placental dysfunction rather than acute hypoxemia. Because movement and tone are controlled by the oldest centers, their loss indicates the most severe compromise, and movement is lost after breathing.

items.stem: A 30-year-old G2P1 woman with diet-controlled gestational diabetes and normal fetal growth is at 38 weeks. When is routine antenatal testing generally started for this condition?
options: At 28 weeks
At 32 weeks
At 36 weeks with twice weekly testing
At 40 weeks
items.explanation: For gestational diabetes well controlled with diet alone and no other complication, antenatal testing is usually started at 40 weeks, with delivery planned by 40 weeks 6 days. Medication-controlled disease or poor control prompts testing from 32 weeks. Testing at 28 weeks is too early for any routine indication. Twice weekly testing at 36 weeks is reserved for higher risk conditions such as restricted growth.

items.stem: A 31-year-old G2P1 woman at 36 weeks with chronic hypertension undergoes a contraction stress test. Late decelerations follow more than half of the contractions, and the baseline variability is moderate. How is this result interpreted, and what does it suggest?
options: A negative test, suggesting a reassuring fetus
A positive test, suggesting uteroplacental insufficiency
An equivocal test requiring only a repeat in one week
An unsatisfactory test because variability is moderate during this pregnancy
items.explanation: A positive contraction stress test is defined by late decelerations following 50 percent or more of contractions, even when the contraction pattern is adequate, and indicates limited placental reserve. A negative test has no late decelerations. Equivocal results involve intermittent late decelerations or variable decelerations. An unsatisfactory test has too few contractions, not moderate variability, and cannot be called unsatisfactory here.

items.stem: A 25-year-old G2P1 woman who teaches kindergarten at 15 weeks has a classmate with erythema infectiosum. Her serology shows parvovirus B19 IgM positive. What is the best surveillance for the fetus?
options: Serial middle cerebral artery Doppler for several weeks
Immediate termination of the pregnancy
Antiviral therapy with acyclovir
Repeat serology only at delivery
items.explanation: Parvovirus B19 infects erythroid precursors and can cause severe fetal anemia and hydrops, most often in the 4 to 8 weeks after maternal infection, so serial Doppler for fetal anemia is advised, with transfusion if needed. Termination is not indicated. Acyclovir has no activity against this virus. Waiting until delivery misses the window to treat anemia.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman with phenylketonuria is at 14 weeks. She has had poor dietary control with a phenylalanine level of 15 mg/dL. Which fetal anomaly is she most at risk of delivering?
options: Duodenal atresia until the next visit
Gastroschisis
Congenital heart disease
Clubfoot
items.explanation: Uncontrolled maternal phenylketonuria causes fetal microcephaly, growth restriction, intellectual disability, and congenital heart defects, so fetal echocardiography is recommended. Good dietary control before conception substantially reduces the risk. Duodenal atresia is associated with Down syndrome, gastroschisis with young maternal age and tobacco use, and clubfoot with a variety of mechanical and genetic causes. The alternatives fail to match the guideline-level recommendation.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes and a hemoglobin A1c of 8.4 percent asks about attempting pregnancy next month. What is the best preconception advice?
options: Conceive now, because control will improve once she is pregnant before any further testing
Stop insulin to reduce fetal exposure
Switch to an oral agent before conception
Delay conception until the hemoglobin A1c is near 6.5 percent or lower
items.explanation: Poor glycemic control at conception raises the rates of congenital anomalies, miscarriage, and stillbirth, so optimizing control before pregnancy, with a target near 6.5 percent when safely achievable, is the main intervention. Hoping control improves later misses the period of organogenesis. Insulin is the safest therapy and must never be stopped in type 1 disease. Oral agents are inadequate for her.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman with epilepsy controlled on valproate plans to conceive in six months. Her seizures have been absent for three years. What is the best preconception management?
options: Change to a safer agent such as lamotrigine and start high-dose folic acid
Continue valproate at the same dose
Stop all antiseizure drugs immediately
Switch to phenytoin and omit folic acid
items.explanation: Valproate carries the highest risk of neural tube defects and neurodevelopmental harm among antiseizure drugs, so a switch to lamotrigine or levetiracetam before conception is preferred, along with folic acid supplementation. Continuing the drug leaves the fetus exposed during organogenesis. Abrupt withdrawal risks seizures that endanger mother and fetus. Phenytoin is also teratogenic and folic acid should not be omitted.

items.stem: A 31-year-old G2P1 woman at 12 weeks had a prior infant with severe neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia and an intracranial hemorrhage. The fetus is again at risk. What is the best antenatal treatment?
options: Platelet transfusion to the mother
Weekly maternal intravenous immune globulin
Anti-D immune globulin injection
Observation until term, then cesarean in the meantime
items.explanation: When a previous sibling had an intracranial hemorrhage, treatment with weekly intravenous immune globulin, with or without corticosteroids, reduces the chance of fetal bleeding by blocking placental transfer of antibody. Maternal platelet transfusion does not help because her count is normal. Anti-D has no role since the target is a platelet antigen. Observation alone risks recurrent hemorrhage before delivery.

items.stem: A 32-year-old G1P0 woman at 17 weeks has a monochorionic diamniotic twin gestation. Which surveillance schedule is recommended for the pregnancy?
options: Ultrasonography every 8 weeks as for dichorionic twins
Single anatomy scan with no further scans until 32 weeks
Ultrasonography every 2 weeks beginning at 16 weeks
Weekly nonstress tests beginning at 20 weeks
items.explanation: Monochorionic twins share a placenta and are at risk of twin-twin transfusion and selective growth restriction, so ultrasound for fluid, bladders, and growth is advised every 2 weeks from 16 weeks. Dichorionic twins are scanned less often, usually every 4 weeks. Skipping scans until 32 weeks would miss transfusion syndrome. Nonstress tests are not used at 20 weeks, because the fetus is not yet reactive.

items.stem: A 25-year-old G1P0 woman at 37 weeks has isolated oligohydramnios with a deepest vertical pocket of 1.5 cm, a normal estimated fetal weight, normal Doppler studies, and intact membranes. What is the best management?
options: Expectant management until 41 weeks
Amnioinfusion with serial scans
Cesarean delivery without a trial of labor until the next visit
Delivery at 36 weeks 0 days to 37 weeks 6 days
items.explanation: Isolated oligohydramnios in a term pregnancy is managed with delivery between 36 weeks 0 days and 37 weeks 6 days according to ACOG guidance, since it is associated with higher stillbirth risk. Waiting until 41 weeks prolongs exposure to that risk. Amnioinfusion is used during labor for variable decelerations, not in this setting. Cesarean delivery is not required and vaginal birth remains reasonable.

items.stem: A 26-year-old G1P0 woman with a prepregnancy BMI of 22 kg/m2 presents at 10 weeks for her first visit and asks how much weight she should gain during a singleton pregnancy. What is the recommended total gain?
options: 25 to 35 pounds
15 to 25 pounds
11 to 20 pounds
35 to 45 pounds
items.explanation: For a normal prepregnancy BMI of 18.5 to 24.9, the recommended total gain is 25 to 35 pounds. The range of 15 to 25 pounds applies to overweight women. The range of 11 to 20 pounds applies to women with obesity. Gaining 35 to 45 pounds exceeds the recommendation and raises the risk of macrosomia, cesarean delivery, and postpartum weight retention.

items.stem: A 37-year-old G1P0 woman at 28 weeks with an uncomplicated pregnancy reports decreased fetal movement for 12 hours. A nonstress test is reactive with normal fluid. What is the best next step?
options: Immediate induction of labor
Hospital admission for continuous monitoring
Reassure and provide guidance on daily fetal movement counting
Repeat the nonstress test every hour for 24 hours in the meantime
items.explanation: A reactive nonstress test and normal amniotic fluid are reassuring, so the patient can go home with instructions to count movements and return if they decrease again. Induction at 28 weeks would cause preterm birth without indication. Continuous admission and hourly testing are excessive for normal results. Counseling about movement patterns remains the key step.

items.stem: A 25-year-old G1P0 woman at 8 weeks takes a daily supplement containing 15,000 international units of preformed vitamin A in addition to her prenatal vitamin. What is the main concern?
options: Folate deficiency from vitamin A
Teratogenicity at high preformed vitamin A intake
Neonatal hemorrhage from vitamin A
Maternal hypocalcemia from vitamin A during this pregnancy
items.explanation: Excess preformed vitamin A (retinol), above about 10,000 international units daily, is associated with craniofacial, cardiac, and central nervous system malformations. Beta-carotene is safe because conversion is regulated. Vitamin A does not interfere with folate absorption and does not cause neonatal bleeding, which is linked to vitamin K deficiency. It also does not cause hypocalcemia.

items.stem: A 23-year-old G1P0 woman at 12 weeks has a routine prenatal screening urine culture that grows more than 100,000 colony-forming units of Escherichia coli. She has no urinary symptoms. What is the best management?
options: Treat with a culture-directed antibiotic and confirm cure
Observe, since she has no symptoms
Treat only if fever or flank pain develops
Give a single dose of antibiotic after delivery before any further testing
items.explanation: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is treated in pregnancy because it progresses to pyelonephritis in a substantial proportion of untreated women, unlike in nonpregnant adults. A test of cure follows therapy. Observation misses the chance to prevent kidney infection and preterm birth. Waiting for symptoms defeats the purpose of screening. A postpartum dose is far too late. Each remaining choice misses the key clinical point here.

items.stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 woman at 35 weeks is sent for a nonstress test because of decreased fetal movement. Which finding defines a reactive tracing at this gestational age?
options: One acceleration of 10 beats per minute for 10 seconds within 10 minutes without further evaluation
A baseline rate above 160 beats per minute
Two accelerations of at least 15 beats per minute for 15 seconds within 20 minutes
Absent variability with late decelerations
items.explanation: At 32 weeks or beyond, a reactive nonstress test requires at least two accelerations of 15 beats per minute lasting 15 seconds in a 20-minute window. Before 32 weeks, the criteria are 10 beats per minute for 10 seconds. A single smaller acceleration does not meet the requirement. A rate above 160 with absent variability and late decelerations is an ominous tracing, not a reassuring one.

items.stem: A 27-year-old G1P0 woman at 10 weeks has a mean corpuscular volume of 66 fL and a normal ferritin. Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows an HbA2 of 5.8 percent, consistent with beta thalassemia trait. What is the next step?
options: Begin high-dose oral iron
Test her partner for hemoglobinopathy
Offer chorionic villus sampling at once
Obtain a fetal echocardiogram
items.explanation: Beta thalassemia trait is benign for the mother, but the fetus can be affected if the father also carries a variant. The next step is to test the partner, and if he is a carrier, offer genetic counseling and prenatal diagnosis. Iron is useless with normal ferritin. Invasive testing before the partner result is premature, and a fetal echocardiogram has no role in this setting.

items.stem: A 24-year-old G1P0 woman at 19 weeks has an ultrasound showing a scalloped frontal bone and a banana-shaped cerebellum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Dandy-Walker malformation with vermian agenesis
Isolated agenesis of the corpus callosum
Holoprosencephaly with fused ventricles
Open spina bifida with Chiari II malformation
items.explanation: The lemon and banana signs result from downward traction on the hindbrain caused by an open neural tube defect and are diagnostic markers for open spina bifida. A Dandy-Walker malformation shows an enlarged posterior fossa with a missing vermis, not a banana shaped cerebellum. Callosal agenesis shows absent cavum septum pellucidum. Holoprosencephaly shows fused midline structures and facial anomalies.

items.stem: A 35-year-old G2P1 woman at 9 weeks 2 days is considering chorionic villus sampling. Which statement about the timing of this procedure is most accurate?
options: It is safest before 8 weeks
It is generally performed between 10 and 13 weeks
It is performed only after 20 weeks
It is performed only with a negative cell-free DNA result
items.explanation: Chorionic villus sampling is usually done at 10 to 13 weeks of gestation. Earlier procedures have been linked with limb reduction defects, which is why sampling before about 10 weeks is avoided. It is not delayed to 20 weeks, a period suited to amniocentesis after 15 weeks. A cell-free DNA test is a screening test and is not a prerequisite for the procedure.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman taking isotretinoin for severe acne asks whether it is safe to stop her contraception because she is planning pregnancy. What is the best counseling?
options: Conceive immediately after stopping the drug
Continue the drug but take extra folic acid
Switch to a topical form during the first trimester only without further evaluation
Stop the drug and wait at least one month before attempting conception
items.explanation: Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen causing craniofacial, cardiac, and central nervous system defects, and women should avoid pregnancy until at least one month after the last dose. Immediate conception risks residual exposure. Folic acid does not prevent retinoid embryopathy. The systemic drug cannot be continued, and topical retinoids are also generally avoided during pregnancy. Each remaining choice misses the key clinical point here.

items.stem: A 29-year-old G1P0 woman with certain dates has an 11-week 0-day pregnancy by her last menstrual period. Crown-rump length measurement shows 12 weeks 2 days. How should the due date be assigned?
options: Redate to the ultrasound measurement
Keep the menstrual dating
Average the two estimates
Repeat the scan in two weeks before deciding
items.explanation: Between 9 weeks 0 days and 13 weeks 6 days, ultrasound dating replaces the menstrual estimate when the difference exceeds 7 days. The discrepancy here is 9 days, which meets that threshold. Keeping the menstrual date would leave the due date wrong, an error that affects later decisions about screening and delivery timing. Averaging is not a recognized method, and repeating the scan adds no accuracy.

items.stem: A 27-year-old G2P1 woman at 17 weeks has a maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein of 3.2 multiples of the median. Her pregnancy was dated by an early ultrasound. What is the best next step?
options: Immediate amniocentesis for karyotype
Repeat the serum test in four weeks
Detailed targeted ultrasonography
Reassurance, because the level is normal
items.explanation: An elevated alpha-fetoprotein, generally 2.0 to 2.5 multiples of the median or above, is associated with open neural tube defects, abdominal wall defects, multiple gestation, and placental abnormalities. A detailed ultrasound is the first step, and amniocentesis is considered only if findings warrant. Repeating the blood test delays diagnosis. A level of 3.2 is not normal.

items.stem: A 30-year-old G1P0 woman at 18 weeks has a quadruple screen with low alpha-fetoprotein, low estriol, low human chorionic gonadotropin, and normal inhibin A. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Trisomy 21 with elevated human chorionic gonadotropin
Trisomy 18
Normal pregnancy with incorrect gestational dating
Fetal anencephaly with high alpha-fetoprotein levels
items.explanation: Trisomy 18 characteristically lowers every marker in the panel, and inhibin A stays near normal. Down syndrome, by contrast, raises human chorionic gonadotropin and inhibin A. Dating error is possible but would shift markers in a predictable way and should be checked, though it does not explain the full low pattern. Anencephaly produces a markedly elevated alpha-fetoprotein, the opposite finding.

items.stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 woman at 12 weeks has cell-free DNA screening that is high risk for trisomy 21. She is anxious and asks whether the result is diagnostic. What is the best response?
options: It is a screening test, and amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling can confirm it
It is diagnostic, so no further testing is needed
It should be repeated in two weeks to confirm
Confirmation requires maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein
items.explanation: Cell-free DNA analysis has a high detection rate but is a screening test, and a positive result needs confirmation by chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis, particularly before any decision about the pregnancy. Calling it diagnostic is wrong because placental mosaicism can cause false positives. Repeating the same test adds no information. Alpha-fetoprotein screens for neural tube defects, not aneuploidy confirmation.

items.stem: A 29-year-old G2P1 woman at 34 weeks has fetal growth restriction with an estimated weight below the third percentile. Umbilical artery Doppler shows absent end-diastolic flow. What is the recommended approach?
options: Continue the pregnancy to 40 weeks with weekly testing
Induce labor immediately regardless of fetal testing
Administer corticosteroids and deliver at about 32 weeks or later with close surveillance
Admit for bed rest and repeat the scan in 4 weeks
items.explanation: Absent end-diastolic flow in a growth-restricted fetus carries a significant risk of stillbirth, and guidance suggests delivery at 32 to 34 weeks, with sooner delivery if testing deteriorates. Prolonging to term is unsafe. Induction without regard to testing is not individualized. Bed rest has no benefit, and a four-week repeat scan misses the window for timely intervention.

items.stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 woman at 21 weeks has an ultrasound showing a double bubble sign in the fetal abdomen with polyhydramnios. Which chromosomal abnormality is most strongly associated with this finding?
options: Trisomy 18
Monosomy X
Triploidy
Trisomy 21
items.explanation: The double bubble sign reflects duodenal atresia, found in about a third of affected fetuses with Down syndrome. Polyhydramnios occurs because the fetus cannot pass swallowed fluid past the obstruction. Trisomy 18 more often shows clenched hands, growth restriction, and heart defects. Monosomy X typically presents with cystic hygroma. Triploidy shows severe early growth restriction and placental changes.

items.stem: A 30-year-old healthy woman with an uncomplicated pregnancy plans an international flight at 30 weeks. Which counseling is most accurate?
options: Flying is contraindicated after 24 weeks
Air travel is acceptable, with walking and hydration during the flight
She should wear no seat belt to avoid abdominal pressure during this pregnancy
Flight is safe only with prophylactic anticoagulation
items.explanation: Commercial air travel is considered safe for healthy pregnant women up to about 36 weeks, and many airlines restrict travel near term. Moving the legs, staying hydrated, and using compression stockings reduce clot risk on long flights. There is no cutoff at 24 weeks. A lap belt should be worn low. Routine anticoagulation is not indicated for a healthy traveler.

items.stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 woman at 16 weeks asks which foods she should avoid to reduce the risk of listeriosis. Which food is the most important to avoid?
options: Soft cheese made from unpasteurized milk
Fully cooked chicken
Pasteurized yogurt
Canned tuna eaten twice weekly in the meantime
items.explanation: Listeria monocytogenes grows in refrigerated foods and causes fetal loss, preterm birth, and neonatal sepsis. Unpasteurized dairy, deli meats not reheated, and smoked refrigerated seafood are the main sources. Thoroughly cooked poultry and pasteurized dairy are safe. Canned light tuna is a mercury consideration, not a listeria concern, and is allowed in limited amounts. The alternatives fail to match the guideline-level recommendation.

items.stem: A 24-year-old G1P0 woman at 20 weeks admits to daily cannabis use and asks whether it is safe. What is the best counseling?
options: Reassure her, because cannabis has no pregnancy effects
Recommend vaping instead of smoking
Suggest switching to edible products
Advise stopping use, because it is associated with adverse fetal outcomes
items.explanation: Cannabis use in pregnancy is associated with lower birth weight and possible neurodevelopmental effects, and the recommendation is to discontinue it, with supportive counseling. Describing it as harmless is inaccurate. Vaping and edible forms still deliver the active compound to the fetus, so changing the route is not a safe alternative. Nonjudgmental screening supports honest disclosure.

items.stem: A 34-year-old G3P2 woman with pregestational diabetes and a hemoglobin A1c of 9.2 percent at conception is at 15 weeks. Which additional study is indicated at 18 to 22 weeks?
options: Amniocentesis for lung maturity
Middle cerebral artery Doppler
Fetal echocardiography
Contraction stress test
items.explanation: Pregestational diabetes with poor early control increases the risk of congenital heart disease and neural tube defects, so fetal echocardiography is recommended in the second trimester. Lung maturity testing is a late-pregnancy concept and rarely used. Middle cerebral artery Doppler assesses anemia. A contraction stress test belongs to third-trimester surveillance and has no role at this gestation.

items.stem: A 38-year-old G2P1 woman, who is Rh negative with a negative antibody screen, undergoes an amniocentesis at 16 weeks. Her partner is Rh positive. What is the best postprocedure management?
options: Check an antibody titer weekly for a month
Administer anti-D immune globulin within 72 hours
Give immune globulin only if bleeding occurs
No treatment, because the fetus is too young to be affected
items.explanation: Amniocentesis can cause fetomaternal hemorrhage, and Rh-negative unsensitized women should receive anti-D immune globulin within 72 hours of the procedure. Titers cannot prevent sensitization. Waiting for bleeding is incorrect because exposure can be silent. Fetal red cells express the D antigen early in gestation, so age of the fetus does not remove the risk. The alternatives fail to match the guideline-level recommendation.

items.stem: A 30-year-old G1P0 woman at 28 weeks has a fetus with sustained supraventricular tachycardia at 240 beats per minute and early signs of hydrops. What is the preferred initial therapy?
options: Transplacental maternal antiarrhythmic therapy such as digoxin or flecainide
Immediate cesarean delivery
Maternal beta-blocker for fetal sedation
Fetal intracardiac injection of adenosine
items.explanation: Fetal tachyarrhythmia with hydrops is treated medically through the mother, typically with digoxin, flecainide, or sotalol, and conversion improves outcome. Delivery at 28 weeks risks prematurity and is a last resort if medical therapy fails. A beta-blocker is not first choice and is not used for sedation. Direct fetal adenosine is an uncommon rescue method rather than a first approach.

items.stem: A 30-year-old G2P1 woman who is Rh(D) negative has a negative antibody screen at 28 weeks, and her partner is Rh positive. What is the most appropriate step?
options: Repeat the antibody screen at 36 weeks only
Give anti-D only after delivery
Start middle cerebral artery Doppler every two weeks
Give anti-D immune globulin 300 micrograms intramuscularly
items.explanation: An unsensitized Rh-negative woman receives anti-D immune globulin at 28 weeks to prevent alloimmunization from silent fetomaternal hemorrhage, with another dose after delivery if the baby is Rh positive. Waiting to repeat the screen offers no protection. Postpartum-only dosing misses antenatal exposure. Doppler surveillance applies to women who are already sensitized, which she is not.

items.stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 woman at 10 weeks smokes a pack of cigarettes daily and wants to quit. Which approach is best at this visit?
options: Nicotine gum for every patient without counseling
Behavioral counseling with a quit line, and pharmacotherapy if counseling fails
Reducing to five cigarettes a day for the pregnancy
Waiting until after delivery to address smoking
items.explanation: Tobacco use raises the risk of growth restriction, preterm birth, abruption, and stillbirth, and behavioral counseling is the first-line intervention, with pharmacotherapy considered when counseling alone fails. Nicotine products without counseling skip the proven foundation. Cutting down only partly reduces harm and is not the goal. Delaying treatment forfeits the benefit of quitting early in pregnancy.

items.stem: A 33-year-old G1P0 woman at 41 weeks 0 days with normal fluid and a reactive nonstress test declines induction and asks about monitoring. What is the best recommendation for the interval to delivery?
options: Wait for spontaneous labor until 44 weeks
Perform testing only if she reports decreased movement during this pregnancy
Antenatal testing, with delivery no later than 42 weeks 0 days
Induce only if the cervix is favorable
items.explanation: Perinatal mortality rises after 41 weeks, and induction is recommended between 41 weeks 0 days and 42 weeks 0 days, with delivery by 42 weeks 0 days. If she declines, twice weekly testing with fluid assessment is reasonable until delivery. Waiting until 44 weeks is unsafe. Testing only after reported symptoms misses silent compromise. Induction can proceed with an unfavorable cervix using ripening agents.

items.stem: A 25-year-old G1P0 woman at 9 weeks has vomited repeatedly for 10 days despite pyridoxine and doxylamine. She has lost 4 percent of her weight and has ketonuria with normal electrolytes. What is the best next step?
options: Immediate termination of this pregnancy
Oral glucocorticoid therapy as first-line treatment
Total parenteral nutrition at the start of treatment
Intravenous fluids and a second antiemetic
items.explanation: Hyperemesis not responding to first-line therapy needs rehydration and a stepwise antiemetic regimen, with thiamine given before dextrose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. Termination is not indicated for a case this mild. Corticosteroids are reserved for refractory disease and carry fetal risk in the first trimester. Parenteral nutrition is a last resort after enteral options fail.

items.stem: A 27-year-old G1P1 woman, 2 days after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery, is found to be rubella nonimmune on her prenatal serology. She is not breastfeeding. What is the best next step?
options: Give the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine before discharge
Give the vaccine at the first prenatal visit of her next pregnancy
Give anti-rubella immune globulin only
Withhold vaccination until she has used contraception for a year
items.explanation: Live attenuated vaccines are contraindicated during pregnancy, so nonimmune women receive the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine in the immediate postpartum period, even while breastfeeding. Waiting for the next pregnancy again forbids vaccination during that pregnancy. Immune globulin does not confer lasting immunity. Only a month of contraception after vaccination is advised, not a year.

items.stem: A 29-year-old G1P0 woman at 10 weeks screens positive as a cystic fibrosis carrier. Her partner has never been tested and has no family history. What is the best next step?
options: Proceed directly to amniocentesis at this visit
Terminate the pregnancy
Offer carrier testing to the partner
Test the fetus only after birth
items.explanation: When one partner is a carrier, testing the other determines the fetal risk. If the partner is negative, residual risk is low but not zero, and if positive, the fetus has a one in four risk of disease and diagnostic testing can be offered. Invasive testing without partner results exposes the pregnancy to risk unnecessarily. Termination is not indicated. Waiting until birth removes options.

items.stem: A 27-year-old G2P1 woman without diabetes is at 39 weeks. Ultrasonography estimates the fetal weight at 4,700 grams. Which counseling is most accurate?
options: Cesarean delivery is considered only if the estimated weight reaches 5,000 grams
Cesarean delivery is mandatory above 4,000 grams
Induction at 37 weeks prevents shoulder dystocia
Ultrasonography weight estimates are accurate within 2 percent
items.explanation: For women without diabetes, planned cesarean delivery may be considered at an estimated fetal weight of at least 5,000 grams, and 4,500 grams for women with diabetes. Ultrasound estimates carry an error of about 15 to 20 percent. A fixed limit of 4,000 grams is not supported. Early induction does not prevent dystocia and raises the rate of cesarean delivery.

items.stem: A 26-year-old G1P0 woman at 12 weeks has opioid use disorder with daily heroin use and asks to stop. What is the recommended management?
options: Medically supervised withdrawal as the first-line approach
Abrupt cessation without medication
Switching to oral oxycodone
Maintenance with methadone or buprenorphine
items.explanation: Opioid agonist therapy with methadone or buprenorphine is standard care in pregnancy, since it reduces relapse, overdose, and fetal stress from repeated withdrawal. Detoxification carries a high relapse rate and risk to the fetus, so it is not the usual first choice. Sudden cessation causes withdrawal that can lead to preterm labor and fetal distress. Prescribing another short-acting opioid does not treat the disorder.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman who has a maternal uncle with fragile X syndrome and intellectual disability asks about carrier testing before pregnancy. What is the best next step?
options: Offer cystic fibrosis screening only
Offer fragile X premutation testing
Reassure, because it is X-linked and she is unaffected
Perform fetal karyotyping during pregnancy
items.explanation: A family history of fragile X or unexplained intellectual disability is an indication for testing for CGG repeat expansion, because women with a premutation can have affected children and ovarian insufficiency. Cystic fibrosis testing does not address this risk. Being unaffected does not exclude carrier status. Standard karyotyping does not detect the repeat expansion and is not the correct test.

items.stem: A 30-year-old G1P0 woman at 22 weeks has a transvaginal cervical length of 18 mm. She has no history of preterm birth and no symptoms. What is the best management?
options: Immediate cerclage placement
Tocolysis with nifedipine for two days
Vaginal progesterone until 36 weeks
Bed rest at home until delivery
items.explanation: For a singleton gestation with no prior spontaneous preterm birth and a short cervix of 25 mm or less before 24 weeks, vaginal progesterone reduces the risk of preterm birth. Cerclage is generally reserved for prior preterm birth or exam-indicated findings. Tocolysis is for active preterm labor. Bed rest has no demonstrated benefit and increases the risk of venous thromboembolism.

items.stem: A 29-year-old G1P0 woman at 28 weeks has an estimated fetal weight at the 5th percentile. Which test best distinguishes a constitutionally small fetus from one with placental insufficiency?
options: Umbilical artery Doppler velocimetry
Maternal serum human chorionic gonadotropin
Amniotic fluid lecithin to sphingomyelin ratio
Cervical length measurement
items.explanation: Umbilical artery Doppler assesses placental resistance, and abnormal waveforms point to placental insufficiency, while normal flow with a small fetus favors a constitutionally small one. Gonadotropin levels do not separate the two. The lecithin to sphingomyelin ratio reflects lung maturity. Cervical length predicts preterm birth risk and is unrelated to fetal growth patterns or placental function.

items.stem: A 20-year-old G1P0 woman at 20 weeks has an anatomy scan showing bowel loops floating freely outside the abdomen to the right of a normal cord insertion, with no covering membrane. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Karyotype is abnormal in most affected fetuses
The defect is covered by a sac of peritoneum
Delivery by cesarean is required for all cases
Chromosomal abnormality is uncommon, and growth is surveilled in the third trimester
items.explanation: This describes gastroschisis, which is usually isolated, associated with young maternal age and tobacco use, and not typically linked to aneuploidy. Third-trimester growth and fluid surveillance are advised because of growth restriction and bowel complications. An abnormal karyotype is typical of omphalocele. A membrane covers an omphalocele, not gastroschisis. Cesarean delivery is reserved for obstetric indications.

items.stem: A 21-year-old G1P0 woman at 9 weeks has a reactive nontreponemal syphilis screen with a titer of 1:16 and a positive treponemal test. She has no symptoms and no known penicillin allergy. What is the best treatment?
options: Oral doxycycline for 14 days
Azithromycin as a single dose
Benzathine penicillin G intramuscularly
Observation with repeat testing at delivery
items.explanation: Penicillin is the only treatment that reliably prevents congenital syphilis, and early latent or primary disease in pregnancy is treated with benzathine penicillin G. Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy. Azithromycin has documented treatment failures and does not reliably cross the placenta. Waiting until delivery would allow fetal infection. Allergic patients undergo desensitization instead. The other options address a different problem or risk harm.

items.stem: A 30-year-old G1P0 woman at 38 weeks has an equivocal biophysical profile of 6 out of 10 with absent breathing movements and normal fluid. What is the best management?
options: Reassure and repeat in one week
Delivery, since the pregnancy is at term
Administer betamethasone for lung maturity
Perform immediate cesarean delivery
items.explanation: A score of 6 is equivocal. At term, the usual response is delivery because the risk of continuing outweighs the benefit, and the route can be vaginal if the fetal status allows. In a preterm fetus, the test is typically repeated within 24 hours. A one-week interval is too long. Steroids are not needed at 38 weeks. A cesarean is not automatic.

items.stem: A 30-year-old G1P0 woman is certain of her last menstrual period, which gives 8 weeks 0 days today. Ultrasonography shows a crown-rump length consistent with 8 weeks 5 days. How should the pregnancy be dated?
options: Redate to the ultrasound, because ultrasound is always more accurate
Redate to the ultrasound only after repeating the scan in two weeks
Keep the menstrual dating
Use the average of the two gestational ages
items.explanation: Before 9 weeks 0 days, the ultrasound date replaces menstrual dating only if the discrepancy exceeds 5 days. Here the difference is exactly 5 days, so the certain menstrual date stands and no change is made. Automatic redating ignores the threshold. Waiting for a repeat scan adds nothing, since dating relies on the first-trimester measurement. Averaging two estimates has no validity in guidelines.

items.stem: A 34-year-old G2P1 woman at 19 weeks has a fetal ultrasound showing bilateral renal agenesis and anhydramnios. What is the expected outcome, and what is the best counseling?
options: Survival with dialysis after delivery
Normal lung development with early surgery at this visit
Resolution with amnioinfusion
Lethal pulmonary hypoplasia, with options counseling
items.explanation: Fetal urine is the main source of amniotic fluid in the second half of pregnancy, and without it the lungs fail to develop, causing Potter sequence and uniformly fatal pulmonary hypoplasia. The family should be counseled about pregnancy options and supportive care. Dialysis does not help because the lungs cannot support life. Amnioinfusion has not produced reliable survival outside research settings.

items.stem: A 32-year-old G3P2 woman at 31 weeks has an amniotic fluid index of 31 cm. A fetal anatomic survey is normal. Which initial test is most appropriate to look for a cause?
options: Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein
Maternal glucose testing
Fetal echocardiography
Maternal toxicology screening
items.explanation: Polyhydramnios is idiopathic in many cases, and the most frequent identifiable cause is maternal diabetes, so glucose testing is the first step along with an anatomic survey. Alpha-fetoprotein is not a standard test at this stage. Fetal echocardiography is reserved for specific indications. Toxicology screening has no connection to fluid volume excess. Other causes include aneuploidy, infection, and fetal anemia.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman at 20 weeks has a routine hemoglobin of 10.3 g/dL and no symptoms. In the second trimester, which hemoglobin value is the usual threshold for diagnosing anemia?
options: Below 10.5 g/dL
Below 9.0 g/dL
Below 11.0 g/dL
Below 12.0 g/dL
items.explanation: Anemia in pregnancy is defined as hemoglobin below 11.0 g/dL in the first and third trimesters and below 10.5 g/dL in the second, reflecting plasma volume expansion that dilutes red cells. Her value of 10.3 therefore qualifies for evaluation. The nonpregnant cutoff of 12.0 does not apply, and 11.0 is a first and third trimester threshold. A cutoff of 9.0 would miss many treatable cases.

items.stem: A 31-year-old G1P0 woman at 20 weeks has an anatomy scan showing an isolated echogenic intracardiac focus. All other anatomy is normal, and her first-trimester screening was low risk. What is the best management?
options: Fetal echocardiography at 24 weeks
Chorionic villus sampling immediately before any further testing
Serial growth scans every two weeks
Reassurance, with no further evaluation
items.explanation: An isolated echogenic intracardiac focus is a common normal variant and is not associated with a meaningful rise in risk after low-risk aneuploidy screening. Echocardiography is not needed, since the focus is not a cardiac structural defect. Invasive testing carries a procedure-related loss risk that outweighs any benefit here. Serial growth scans are not indicated for this finding.

items.stem: A 32-year-old G1P0 woman at 12 weeks has a nuchal translucency of 4.2 mm. Chorionic villus sampling shows a normal 46,XX karyotype. What is the best next step?
options: Routine care without further evaluation
Repeat cell-free DNA screening at 20 weeks
Detailed anatomy ultrasonography and fetal echocardiography
Termination counseling for a presumed syndrome at this visit before any further testing
items.explanation: An enlarged nuchal translucency raises the risk of structural heart defects and genetic syndromes even with a normal karyotype, so a detailed anatomy scan and fetal echocardiogram are advised, with consideration of microarray. Routine care ignores that risk. Cell-free DNA adds nothing after a diagnostic result. Termination counseling is premature when the cause is unknown and many fetuses are normal.

items.stem: A 26-year-old G1P0 woman at 21 weeks has an ultrasound showing the fetal stomach and bowel in the chest, a mediastinal shift, and a small abdominal circumference. What is the major determinant of neonatal outcome in this condition?
options: Degree of pulmonary hypoplasia
Maternal age at delivery
Presence of polyhydramnios alone
Fetal sex
items.explanation: A congenital diaphragmatic hernia allows abdominal organs to compress the developing lung, and the resulting pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension determine survival. The lung-to-head ratio and liver position are used to estimate severity. Maternal age and fetal sex do not drive prognosis. Polyhydramnios can occur but does not define outcome, and the severity of lung compression remains the dominant factor.

items.stem: A 29-year-old G1P0 woman at 20 weeks has an anatomy scan showing an isolated single umbilical artery with normal fetal anatomy. What is the best management?
options: Fetal karyotype by amniocentesis
Growth ultrasonography in the third trimester
Immediate delivery planning at 34 weeks until the next visit
Repeat anatomy scan every 2 weeks
items.explanation: An isolated single umbilical artery is present in about 1 percent of pregnancies and is associated with a modest rise in growth restriction, so a growth scan in the third trimester is advised. Karyotyping is unnecessary without other findings. Early delivery has no role. Frequent anatomy scans add no value, since the vessel count will not change over time.

items.stem: A 27-year-old G2P1 woman at 21 weeks has fetal ventriculomegaly with an atrial width of 13 mm on anatomy ultrasonography. What is the best next step?
options: Reassurance and routine care
Immediate shunt placement in the fetus
Karyotype or microarray, infection testing, and fetal magnetic resonance imaging
Delivery at 34 weeks
items.explanation: An atrial diameter of 10 to 12 mm is mild and 15 mm or more is severe, and 13 mm is moderate, which warrants a thorough evaluation for chromosomal abnormality, congenital infection, and structural brain anomalies with magnetic resonance imaging. Routine care ignores the risk of neurologic disability. Fetal shunting is not an established therapy. Early delivery is not indicated.

items.stem: A 32-year-old G2P1 woman at 26 weeks with a complete placenta previa and recurrent bleeding asks about her exercise routine. What is the best advice?
options: Avoid vigorous exercise because of the previa and bleeding
Continue running as before, because exercise is always safe
Begin heavy lifting to maintain strength
Perform hot yoga to relax
items.explanation: Exercise is encouraged in uncomplicated pregnancy, but persistent second-trimester bleeding, placenta previa after 26 weeks, preterm labor risk, and severe preeclampsia are absolute contraindications to vigorous activity. Saying that exercise is always safe overlooks these conditions. Heavy lifting raises intra-abdominal pressure. Hot yoga risks hyperthermia, which is a concern in any pregnancy, and is not advised.

items.stem: A 26-year-old G3P2 woman at 24 weeks who is Rh negative has an anti-D titer of 1:32 and no prior affected infant. What is the best next step in management?
options: Repeat titers every week and deliver at 32 weeks before any further testing
Serial middle cerebral artery Doppler measurements
Immediate amniocentesis for fetal Rh status only
Give anti-D immune globulin to lower the titer
items.explanation: A titer at or above the critical threshold (commonly 1:16) in a woman with no prior affected pregnancy indicates a risk of fetal anemia, and serial middle cerebral artery Doppler is the preferred noninvasive surveillance method. Titers alone cannot guide timing. Fetal typing is useful but does not assess anemia. Immune globulin prevents sensitization and does not treat established antibodies.

items.stem: A 22-year-old G1P0 woman at 20 weeks has an ultrasound showing a midline anterior abdominal wall defect with the liver and bowel herniating into a membrane-covered sac at the cord insertion. What is the best next step?
options: Reassurance, because this is usually an isolated finding
Emergent delivery at 28 weeks
Maternal serum testing for infection
Fetal karyotype and detailed anatomic survey
items.explanation: A covered sac containing liver describes an omphalocele, which is associated with aneuploidy, especially trisomy 18, and with syndromes such as Beckwith-Wiedemann and cardiac defects. Gastroschisis, by contrast, has uncovered bowel to the right of the cord and is usually isolated. Early delivery is not indicated. Maternal infection testing is not the cause here. Each remaining choice misses the key clinical point here.

items.stem: A 31-year-old G2P1 woman with a BMI of 33 kg/m2 is at 14 weeks. She asks whether she should try to lose weight during pregnancy. What is the best counseling?
options: Aim for a gain of 25 to 35 pounds like any other woman
Restrict calories to below 1,200 per day until delivery at this visit
Aim for a gain of 11 to 20 pounds and avoid intentional weight loss
Aim for no net weight change throughout pregnancy
items.explanation: Women with obesity should gain less than average, 11 to 20 pounds, and should not diet to lose weight, which risks ketosis and inadequate nutrition. Using the normal-weight target of 25 to 35 pounds promotes excess gain. Severe calorie restriction is unsafe for the fetus. A rule of zero net change is not a guideline target and may be reasonable only in special cases under supervision.

items.stem: A 30-year-old G2P1 woman at 18 weeks has a positive antibody screen. Identification shows anti-Lewis antibodies only. Which statement about the fetal risk is correct?
options: Hemolytic disease of the newborn is unlikely
Severe hydrops is expected by 24 weeks
Intrauterine transfusion will be required at this visit
Delivery should be planned at 34 weeks
items.explanation: Lewis antibodies are generally of the IgM class and do not cross the placenta, and the antigens are poorly expressed on fetal red cells, so hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn is not a concern. Clinically significant antibodies such as anti-D, anti-Kell, and anti-c do cross and cause disease. Hydrops, transfusion, and early delivery apply to those antibodies, not to this one.

items.stem: A 28-year-old G1P0 woman at 22 weeks is counseled about prenatal open repair of a fetal myelomeningocele. Which maternal condition would exclude her from this surgery?
options: Fetal gestational age of 23 weeks
Normal fetal karyotype
Singleton pregnancy
Previous classical hysterotomy with a uterine scar
items.explanation: Open fetal surgery requires a singleton fetus with a normal karyotype, a lesion between T1 and S1 with hindbrain herniation, and gestational age between 19 weeks 0 days and 25 weeks 6 days. A prior classical hysterotomy raises the risk of uterine rupture and is an exclusion. A gestation of 23 weeks and a normal karyotype are requirements rather than barriers.

items.stem: A 33-year-old G3P2 woman at 26 weeks has a fetus with nonimmune hydrops. Ultrasonography shows ascites, a pleural effusion, and skin edema, with no structural anomaly. Which maternal test is part of the initial evaluation?
options: Serum prolactin level
Antibody screen and Kleihauer-Betke testing
Pelvic computed tomography
Cervical culture for gonorrhea during this pregnancy
items.explanation: The initial work-up of hydrops includes confirming the absence of red cell alloimmunization, testing for fetal-maternal hemorrhage, infection serologies such as parvovirus and syphilis, and fetal karyotype or microarray. Prolactin has no role. Computed tomography exposes the fetus to radiation and does not help. A cervical culture for gonorrhea is not part of the hydrops evaluation.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman reports a last menstrual period of March 10 with regular 28-day cycles. Using Naegele rule, what is her estimated due date?
options: December 17 of the same year
December 10 of the same year
December 3 of the same year
January 10 of the following year
items.explanation: Naegele rule adds one year, subtracts three months, and adds seven days to the first day of the last menstrual period. March 10 becomes December 10, then December 17. Omitting the seven days gives December 10. Subtracting a further week gives an early date that is unsupported. Adding nine months without the seven-day adjustment, as in the January option, is incorrect.

items.stem: A 22-year-old G1P0 woman at 8 weeks attends her first prenatal visit. She has no known risk factors for HIV and asks whether testing is necessary. What is the recommended approach?
options: Test only women reporting high-risk behavior
Test only in the third trimester
Offer HIV testing to all pregnant women, with an opt-out approach
Test only with the written consent of her partner
items.explanation: Universal HIV screening is recommended at the first prenatal visit using an opt-out strategy, since treatment in pregnancy reduces perinatal transmission to below one percent. Risk-based testing misses a large share of infections. Testing only late wastes the opportunity for early treatment. Partner consent is not required, and women may decline testing on their own.

items.stem: A 33-year-old G3P2 woman at 22 weeks asks whether she can receive the seasonal influenza vaccine, because the season has just begun. Which statement is correct?
options: Vaccination should wait until the second trimester has ended
Inactivated vaccine is recommended in any trimester
The live intranasal vaccine is preferred
Vaccination is contraindicated while she is pregnant
items.explanation: Inactivated influenza vaccine is recommended for all pregnant women during influenza season at any gestational age, because pregnancy increases the risk of severe illness and the vaccine protects the newborn through antibody transfer. The live intranasal formulation is contraindicated in pregnancy. Delaying to the third trimester withholds protection during a vulnerable period. It is not contraindicated.

items.stem: A 30-year-old G2P1 woman has a last menstrual period consistent with 18 weeks 0 days. A first scan today estimates 17 weeks 0 days. What is the correct dating decision?
options: Redate to 17 weeks 0 days
Redate to 18 weeks 3 days
Use the biparietal diameter alone for dating
Retain the menstrual due date
items.explanation: From 16 weeks 0 days to 21 weeks 6 days, the ultrasound estimate replaces the menstrual date only when the difference is more than 10 days. A 7-day difference falls inside that margin, so the certain menstrual dating stays. Redating to the ultrasound value would apply a threshold meant for the first trimester. Relying on a single biometric parameter reduces accuracy compared with the composite estimate.
